rv.q: That’s more than a wicked valentine: It’s a vision.
Rebeck draws a portrait of backstage camaraderie, artistic anxiety and 19th Century celebrity that's both convincing and charming.
And blazing stars they certainly are, both McTeer and Bernhardt, yoked in a dynamic character study that, for all its shining moments, is no play.
When the play sticks to the words that reside on the marquee — that would be 'Bernhardt-slash-Hamlet'
Though McTeer gives a magnetic, precise performance, the play itself meanders
While it is sometimes ungainly, the play is amusing on its own inside-theater terms.
However, the play in most respects is a missed opportunity, despite the pleasure of watching the willowy, silver-tongued McTeer careen from high camp into righteous hauteur.
The badass British actor Janet McTeer, for all her innate playfulness and power, can’t save this reincarnation of the Divine Sarah.
The result is the worst of both worlds, a preachy backstage farce.

"As enjoyable as the play is, the thunderous ovation at the end of these 2 ½ hours is primarily for the dazzlingly brilliant Janet McTeer. Guided by the savvy director Moritz von Stuelpnagel, the Tony-winning star makes not just a meal but an entire tasting menu out of the central role of the celebrated French actress Sarah Bernhardt.
She's also the best, most vivid thing in nearly every scene.
As soon as the lights go up and she begins soliloquizing—“Oh what a rogue and peasant slave am I!”—we are immediately, completely, utterly, spellbound.
Regardless of the title, the soul gripping center of this show is Janet McTeer, and what a whirlwind she is.
Director Daniel Sullivan hits just the right tone of contained insanity and arch cynicism.
“Bernhardt/Hamlet” deserves to be seen twice and revived often.

“McTeer is luminous...Two of 'Bernhardt/Hamlet''s themes, the challenges of performing Hamlet and women's constant battle against a sexist society, are well presented...The story of the great romance between Bernhardt and Rostand, that is underwritten.
Teresa Rebeck's new play now getting a classy premiere production at the Roundabout's Theatre captures the star power of both its main character and her interpreter.

Yes, there's some damn good, expressive and provocative writing in Bernhardt/Hamlet, and the opportunity to see an exceptional artist like McTeer draw every complex nuance out Rebeck's best words is an experience worthy of any Broadway season.
Act 2 is where the story finally gathers its momentum and the meticulously placed pieces from Act 1 realign in ways that offer insight.
Any of these might be enough to sustain a play, but the way Rebeck strings them together makes this almost two-and-a-half-hour production feel too slight.
Bernhardt/Hamlet winds up using Shakespeare neither for high art (a la Tom Stoppard’s Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead) nor low farce (a la Something Rotten), but as a middle brow entertainment.
By the second act, the play becomes tiresome and feels long-winded.
What is lacking in Bernhardt/Hamlet is a strong plot, a reason to move forward, something that raises the stakes.
Enjoy Bernhardt/Hamlet for what it is but the play ultimately seems less than the sum of its parts.
That’s to say she does what the best actors do under these conditions: she raises the dramaturgical level without entirely saving the proceedings.
One cannot argue with Rebeck's premise. One can only wish she'd written a better play.
While topically resonant, "Bernhardt/Hamlet" is dramatically inert.
McTeer's tour de force performance lays bare the flaws, foibles and fortunes of the premiere actress of her day.
Janet McTeer is a treasure, commanding the stage like few others these days.
Brilliantly, Janet McTeer exhibits this extravagant personality at this one point in her life.
A terrifically theatrical and entertaining but not quite airtight new Broadway comedy.
McTeer gives a great performance.
If nothing else, Janet McTeer has here proven how true her line is: women deserve difficult roles, given them a chance and they will soar.
Bernhardt/Hamlet is a lumpy but often enjoyable play about a theatrical legend, with a feminist message that our current generation will appreciate.
Likewise, handsome period costumes by Toni-Leslie James couple with fine performances throughout to make “Bernhardt/Hamlet” watchable, despite its illegibility.
All in all, it was a disappointment.

cn.t: Critics praise Janet McTeer's magnetic performance as Sarah Bernhardt, but find Theresa Rebeck's play overwritten and dramatically uneven.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
